summary: Analyzes the history of how transient numeric identifiers were specified and implemented in IETF protocols and how security and privacy suffered. It provides evidence that guidance is needed. It is a product of the Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: Many protocols carry a number that only has to be unique for a while, such as the packet ID in IPv4 or the first sequence number in a TCP connection. If those numbers follow a predictable pattern, someone who cannot see your traffic can still guess them, and use the guess to inject data, blind you, or follow your device around the network. This RFC shows how the same failure has been rediscovered in protocol after protocol since 1981.

subtitle: How weak choices of transient identifiers kept producing the same failures for more than thirty years.

tldr.problem: For more than 30 years, IETF protocols have used transient numeric identifiers, such as IP Identification values, TCP initial sequence numbers and port numbers, whose predictable choice led to denial of service, data injection and information leakage.
tldr.mechanism: This document traces a timeline of specification and vulnerability disclosure for a sample of these identifiers and shows that the recurring cause is a specification that under-specifies, over-specifies or is not implemented as written.
tldr.outcome: The analysis is the evidence behind two companion documents: RFC 9415 gives sample generation algorithms and RFC 9416 requires future specifications to state interoperability requirements, assess vulnerabilities and recommend an algorithm.

facts.label: Years from ISN attack to RFC 793 update

today: RFC 9414 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It is the historical record behind two companion documents: RFC 9415, which gives sample generation algorithms, and RFC 9416, which requires future IETF specifications to state interoperability requirements, assess vulnerabilities and recommend an algorithm.

sections.title: The Same Mistake, Repeated
sections.content:
Networking protocols use a variety of transient numeric identifiers for different protocol objects: IPv4 and IPv6 Identification values, IPv6 Interface Identifiers, transport-protocol ephemeral port numbers, TCP Initial Sequence Numbers, NTP Reference IDs and DNS IDs. These identifiers usually have requirements, such as uniqueness during a specified period, that must be met without negative interoperability consequences and without an associated failure severity when they are not met.

For more than 30 years a large number of implementations of IETF protocols have been subject to attacks with effects ranging from denial of service and data injection to information leakage that could be exploited for pervasive monitoring. The root cause of these issues has in many cases been the poor selection of transient numeric identifiers, usually as a result of insufficient or misleading specifications. While it is generally trivial to identify an algorithm that satisfies the interoperability requirements of a given identifier, empirical evidence exists that doing so without harming the security or privacy properties of the protocol is prone to error. Implementations have been subject to issues from predictable IPv4 and IPv6 Identification values, predictable IPv6 interface identifiers, predictable ephemeral port numbers, predictable TCP initial sequence numbers, predictable initial timestamps in the TCP timestamps option, and predictable DNS IDs.

Recent history indicates that when new protocols are standardized or new implementations are produced, the security and privacy properties of the associated identifiers tend to be overlooked, and inappropriate algorithms are either suggested in the specifications or chosen by implementors.

The document contains a non-exhaustive timeline of the specification and vulnerability disclosures for a sample of these identifiers, and it draws three conclusions. Vulnerabilities associated with inappropriate generation of transient numeric identifiers have affected protocol implementations for an extremely long time. Such vulnerabilities, even when addressed for a given protocol version, were later reintroduced in new versions or new implementations of the same protocol. And standardization efforts that discuss and provide advice in this area can have a positive effect on IETF specifications and their corresponding implementations. The document represents the consensus of the Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The pattern repeats. A protocol needs a number that is only unique for a short time, the specification says little or says too much about how to pick it, implementers choose something simple, and someone finds a way to abuse it. Fixing one protocol does not stop the next one from making the same mistake, which is why this RFC ends with a process requirement rather than a patch.

sections.title: What Counts as a Transient Identifier
sections.content:
A transient numeric identifier is a data object in a protocol specification that can be used to definitely distinguish a protocol object, such as a datagram, network interface, transport-protocol endpoint or session, from all other objects of the same type in a given context. These identifiers are usually defined as a series of bits and represented using integer values, and are typically dynamically selected, as opposed to statically assigned numeric identifiers. Different identifiers may have additional requirements depending on their specific use in a protocol. The document uses the term as a generic name for any data object satisfying that identification property. The terms constant IID, stable IID and temporary IID are to be interpreted as defined in RFC 7721.

The threat model is deliberately narrow. On-path attacks are not considered: the attacker is assumed not to have physical or logical access to the systems being attacked, and can only observe traffic explicitly directed to the attacker. The attacker cannot observe traffic transferred between the sender and the receivers of a target protocol, but may be able to interact with any of these entities, for example by sending traffic to them to sample the transient numeric identifiers those hosts use when talking to the attacker.

Applied to TCP initial sequence numbers, the attacker is unable to capture the traffic of a TCP connection between two other hosts, but is able to establish a TCP connection with any of them to sample the sequence numbers they use. Applied to IPv6 interface identifiers, the attacker may learn a victim's IPv6 address if it becomes exposed, for example when the victim talks to an attacker-operated server, and can then track the host by probing a set of addresses built from target prefixes and the learned interface identifier. None of these scenarios require the attacker to observe traffic not explicitly directed to it.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is careful about what the attacker can see. The attacker is off the path: it cannot watch your traffic to a third party, but it can talk to your machine and see what your machine sends. That is enough to learn the pattern of the numbers your machine picks, and that is the whole point of the exercise.

sections.title: Three Ways a Specification Goes Wrong
sections.content:
Most of the problems in this document come from one of three conditions: protocol specifications that under-specify their transient numeric identifiers, specifications that over-specify them, and implementations that fail to comply with the specified requirements.

Under-specification led to implementations vulnerable to numerous off-path attacks. Examples are the specification of TCP local ports in RFC 793 and the specification of the DNS ID in RFC 1035, neither of which said enough about how to choose the value. The TCP local port in an active OPEN request is commonly known as the ephemeral port of the connection.

Over-specification also happened. RFC 4291 essentially overloads the semantics of IPv6 interface identifiers by embedding link-layer addresses in them, when the uniqueness requirement could be met in other ways that do not carry the same security and privacy cost. Similarly, RFC 2460 suggests the use of a global counter for generating IPv6 Identification values, when the requirement of uniqueness per {IPv6 Source Address, IPv6 Destination Address} could be met by other algorithms without the same cost.

Finally, some implementations simply fail to comply. Some popular operating systems still fail to implement transport-protocol ephemeral port randomization, as recommended in RFC 6056, or TCP initial sequence number randomization, as recommended in RFC 9293.

The document closes by pointing at the two companion documents that answer these problems. RFC 9415 analyzes and categorizes transient numeric identifiers by their interoperability requirements and failure severities, and recommends algorithms that meet those requirements without harming security or privacy. RFC 9416 formally requires IETF protocol specifications to state the interoperability requirements for their transient numeric identifiers, to carry out a warranted vulnerability assessment, and to recommend algorithms for generating them so that the requirements are met while negative security or privacy properties are mitigated.
sections.plainLanguage: Three failure modes explain the record. Say too little and implementers invent something predictable. Say too much and you lock in a bad method that could have been avoided. Or write a good rule and have implementers ignore it. The two documents that followed from this RFC turn the lesson into a requirement: every new specification must say how the number is chosen, must assess the risk, and must recommend an algorithm.

sections.title: The IP Identification Field
sections.content:
The IPv4 Identification field, specified in RFC 791, must be unique for a given {Source Address, Destination Address, Protocol} for as long as the datagram or any fragment of it could be alive in the Internet. The specification suggests that a sending protocol module may keep a table of identifiers, one entry for each destination it has communicated with in the last maximum packet lifetime, and that since the field allows 65,536 different values, hosts may be able to use unique identifiers independent of destination. This has been interpreted many times as a suggestion to use per-destination or global counters. The specification does not suggest any flawed algorithm, but it omits any discussion of the security and privacy implications of predictable values, and many IPv4 implementations ended up generating them with a global counter.

The IPv6 Identification was originally specified in RFC 1883. It serves the same purpose, but sits in the Fragment Header rather than the base header. RFC 1883 states that the Identification must differ from that of any other fragmented packet sent recently with the same source and destination address, and that this can be met with a wrap-around 32-bit counter incremented each time a packet must be fragmented, leaving it an implementation choice whether to use a global or per-destination counter. The suggestion is more explicit than in the IPv4 case. RFC 2460, the first revision of the core IPv6 specification, kept the same text. RFC 8200, the second revision, removes the counter suggestion and points to RFC 7739 for sample algorithms, but still does not introduce security and privacy requirements on the generation of IPv6 Identification values.

The consequences arrived in stages. In December 1998, work showed that predictable IPv4 Identification values, as generated by most popular implementations, can be used to count the packets a target node sends, and that the same weakness supports a port-scanning technique known as idle scan, whose tool was publicly released. In November 1999, the same weakness was shown to reveal the rules of a number of firewalls. In September 2002, the idle scan technique was documented in the popular Network Mapper tool. In November 2002, the Identification field was shown to be exploitable to count the number of systems behind a NAT. In December 2003, a technique for TCP data injection attacks based on predictable IPv4 Identification values was described, requiring less effort than injection with bare TCP packets. In October 2007, a weakness was described in the pseudorandom number generator used by a number of operating systems for IP Identification values, and in June 2011 the idle scan was shown to work against IPv6.

Mitigation took a long time and was repeatedly weakened. OpenBSD implemented randomization of the IPv4 Identification field in December 1998 and of the IPv6 one in October 2003; Linux mitigated predictable IPv6 Identification values in November 2011. A 2011 draft describing the security implications of predictable IPv6 Identification values was intended to update RFC 2460, but in December 2014 the working group changed its intended status to Informational, which meant it no longer formally updated RFC 2460 and the security and privacy requirements on the generation of IPv6 Identification values were eliminated. RFC 7739 in February 2016 analysed the implications and provided guidance for selecting a generation algorithm, but as an Informational RFC it did not formally update RFC 2460 and introduced no requirements. RFC 8200 followed in July 2017. In October 2019 the IPv6 Identification generators of two popular operating systems were reported to be flawed.
sections.plainLanguage: The Identification field in an IPv4 packet exists so that fragments of the same packet can be recognised. The original specification mentioned counters, and many systems used one. A counter is guessable, and a guessable Identification lets an attacker count the packets a host sends, scan ports through it, see how many machines sit behind a NAT, or inject data into a connection. Randomising the field fixed it in practice, but the specification was never formally changed to require it.

sections.title: TCP Sequence Numbers and IPv6 Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
RFC 793 suggests that the choice of the initial sequence number of a connection is not arbitrary but aims to reduce the chances of a stale segment being accepted by a new incarnation of a previous connection. It suggests a global 32-bit generator incremented by 1 roughly every 4 microseconds. In practice, protection against stale segments is enforced by preventing a new incarnation before twice the maximum segment lifetime has passed since a segment of the old incarnation was last seen, using the TIME-WAIT state and TCP's quiet time. Based on the assumption that initial sequence numbers increase monotonically across connections, many stacks use the sequence number of an incoming SYN to run heuristics that allow a new incarnation while the previous one is still in TIME-WAIT, which avoids an interoperability problem when a node connects to a specific endpoint at a high rate.

A global counter makes the sequence number trivial to predict, which allows a range of attacks. February 1985 saw the first description of exploiting predictable initial sequence numbers to forge TCP connections that could then be leveraged for trust relationship exploitation; April 1989 brought the security considerations for predictable initial sequence numbers. In January 1995 a real-world exploitation of the 1985 attack was reported, ten years after the original work. The first IETF effort to address the problem, RFC 1948 in May 1996, was authored by Steven Bellovin but did not formally update RFC 793. OpenBSD implemented randomization based on random increments in July 1996 and on simple randomization in December 2000. A March 2001 analysis documented statistical weaknesses in some generators, with vulnerability advisories released for popular implementations, and a March 2002 update concluded that many vendors had either ignored the issue or implemented a flawed solution that appeared not to have been tested with a known approach. RFC 6528, published in February 2012 and 27 years after the original work, formally updated RFC 793 to mitigate predictable initial sequence numbers. In August 2014 the RFC 6528 algorithm became the recommended algorithm in a draft revision of the core TCP specification, and RFC 9293, published in August 2022, adopted it.

IPv6 interface identifiers come from several mechanisms, including stateless address autoconfiguration, DHCPv6 and manual configuration. The document focuses on those from stateless address autoconfiguration. The interface identifier of stable IPv6 addresses originally resulted from the underlying link-layer address being embedded in it, which was seen as a convenient way to obtain a unique address. Awareness of the security and privacy cost of that approach led to its replacement with an alternative that does not affect those properties.

The history runs from January 1997, when RFC 2073 recommended generating addresses using link-specific addresses as interface identifiers such as 48-bit IEEE 802 MAC addresses, through July 1998, when RFC 2374 required IIDs in IEEE 64-bit Extended Unique Identifier format, to February 2006, when RFC 4291 required the Modified EUI-64 format for all unicast addresses except those starting with the binary value 000. January 2001 brought RFC 3041, which recognised the problem of IPv6 network activity correlation and specified IPv6 temporary addresses. In March 2008 RFC 5157 gave hints on how patterns in IPv6 addresses could be leveraged for address scanning, and in December 2011 a draft noted that the original scheme allowed IPv6 address scanning and active host tracking even when temporary addresses were employed. That draft stopped short of formally updating RFC 4291, so the specified algorithm never formally replaced Modified EUI-64 identifiers. RFC 7217 in April 2014 specified a method for generating semantically opaque interface identifiers as an alternative to, but not a replacement for, Modified EUI-64 format identifiers. RFC 7707 and RFC 7721 on network reconnaissance in IPv6 and on security and privacy considerations for IPv6 address generation were published in March 2016, and RFC 8064 in February 2017 recommended the RFC 7217 algorithm and formally updated a large number of RFCs. Finally RFC 8981, published in February 2021 after approval in December 2020, addressed the flaws in RFC 4941 by revising it.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP's first sequence number had the same problem: a fixed-rate counter makes it predictable, and a predicted sequence number lets an attacker forge a connection. It took 27 years from the first published attack to the specification being updated. IPv6 had a related problem with the address of an interface: embedding the hardware address in it let anyone scan for hosts and follow them across networks, and the fix took a similar long road.

sections.title: Time Sources, Ports and DNS
sections.content:
NTP Reference IDs. The NTP Reference ID is a 32-bit code identifying the particular server or reference clock. Above stratum 1 it can be used to avoid degree-one timing loops, where two NTP peers are each other's time source. In the IPv4 address family the identifier is the four-octet IPv4 address of the time source; in the IPv6 address family it is the first four octets of the MD5 hash of the IPv6 address. RFC 5905 was published in June 2010. In July 2016 a draft described the information leakage produced through the REFID and proposed that NTP return a special REFID when a packet uses a source address that is not believed to be a current NTP peer. It was adopted by the NTP working group, but in April 2019 the proposal was judged sub-optimal and, for lack of working group support, the effort was abandoned.

Ephemeral port numbers. Most transport protocols use port numbers to demultiplex packets to the right transport instance, and ephemeral ports are the local ports used in active OPEN requests, that is, typically the local ports on the side initiating the communication. RFC 768 notes that the UDP source port is optional and identifies the sending process, but specifies no interoperability requirements for source port selection and suggests no way to select ports; most popular implementations ended up choosing source ports from a system-wide global counter. RFC 793 describes the use of port numbers and requires that they yield a unique socket pair of {local address, local port, remote address, remote port}, but leaves how ephemeral ports are selected, and the range they are chosen from, unspecified. OpenBSD implemented ephemeral port randomization in July 1996.

The consequences were concrete. In July 2008 the CERT Coordination Center published details of what became known as the Kaminsky attack on DNS, exploiting the lack of ephemeral port randomization and DNS ID randomization in many major DNS implementations to poison caches in an effective and practical manner. RFC 5452 in January 2009 mandated port randomization for DNS resolvers, and mandated that implementations randomize ports from the range of available ports, 53 or 1024 and above, as large as possible and practicable, without recommending an algorithm; it led to port randomization in the DNS resolvers themselves rather than in the underlying transport protocols. RFC 6056 in January 2011 noted that many TCP and UDP implementations produce predictable ephemeral port numbers and select them from a small portion of the port number space, recommended implementing ephemeral port randomization, proposed algorithms, and recommended randomizing over the range 1024 to 65535. In March 2016 a report described a non-normal distribution of the ephemeral port numbers used by the NTP clients of an Internet Time Service. A 2019 draft noted that some NTP implementations use the NTP service port 123 as the local port for nonsymmetric modes; it met some pushback in the working group but was eventually adopted and published as RFC 9109 in August 2021.

The DNS ID. The DNS ID, sometimes called the query ID or TxID, matches DNS replies to outstanding queries. RFC 1035, published in November 1987, specified it as a 16-bit identifier assigned by the program that generates a query, copied into the reply, without specifying interoperability requirements or suggesting a generation algorithm. In August 1993 cache poisoning attacks requiring the attacker to guess the DNS ID were described. In June 1995 it was suggested that both the UDP source port and the DNS ID of query packets should be randomised, though with a note that this might not provide enough entropy to prevent guessing. April 1997 work found implementations using predictable UDP source ports and predictable DNS IDs, and argued that both should be randomised. In November 2002 it was shown that spoofing multiple requests for the same domain name from different IP addresses lets an attacker guess the DNS ID with a high probability of success. In March 2007 the Microsoft Windows DNS server was found to generate predictable DNS IDs, and in July 2007 a DNS server that did randomise the ID was still subject to cache poisoning by forging many queries and exploiting the birthday paradox. In October 2007 OpenBSD's DNS software was found to generate predictable IDs. RFC 5452 in January 2009 required resolvers to randomise the DNS ID and to check that a reply's ID matches the query. In May 2010 the Windows SMTP Service was found to run its own resolver with predictable DNS IDs and to fail to validate that a reply's ID matched the query that supposedly elicited it.
sections.plainLanguage: Three more identifiers show the same story. The NTP reference ID reveals which clock a server is using, which leaks information about the network. Ephemeral port numbers chosen from a counter let an attacker find and target a machine without seeing any traffic. And the DNS query ID, a 16-bit number copied into the reply, let an attacker poison a resolver's cache by guessing it, which is how a whole family of DNS attacks worked.
